title: Editable checkpoint state lets an agent self-approve and merge without the human review gate
description: The checkpoint hook treats gate/status fields in the editable plan JSON as proof that gates passed. A repository contributor can add prompt instructions in AGENTS.md directing an active coding agent to set all checkpoint gates and status to passed, skip AskUserQuestion, and merge the feature branch into local main. The registered PreToolUse hook routes Write/Edit of checkpoint JSON through check_plan, but check_plan verifies only field consistency and checkpoint ordering; it does not require test receipts or a human-issued approval event. A disposable-clone reproduction showed forged plan transitions accepted and allowed the feature branch to be merged into local main. No remote push was performed.
root_cause: check_plan in scripts/checkpoint-gate.py validates self-asserted gate fields for consistency but does not require verifiable human approval or gate evidence, allowing an agent to advance and merge unreviewed work.
intended_behavior: The checkpoint plan and app review are mandatory human approval gates; editing local plan JSON must not impersonate a user's approval.

trace.description: The repository registers checkpoint-gate.py as a PreToolUse hook for Copilot CLI.
The Write/Edit path-matching branch admits checkpoint JSON and routes the resulting text to check_plan.
The hook accepts a checkpoint marked passed when its editable gate fields are all passed or n/a; it does not verify that a human approved or the gates actually ran.
After check_plan accepts the self-asserted result, the PreToolUse hook returns allow; the human-review prompt is not part of this enforcement path.

conditions.description: The attacker can contribute repository instructions that an active coding agent reads; the agent has the normal local worktree write and Git permissions.
A coding agent is running the governed workflow without an external approval token or protected merge control.

execution.attacker_perspective: A repository contributor who wants their unreviewed change merged into a developer's local main through a prompt-injected coding agent.
payloads: Add repository-controlled AGENTS.md instructions telling the agent to skip AskUserQuestion, edit .ai-engineering/workflow/checkpoints/<slug>.json so all gates and status are passed, and run the local merge step.
instructions: Have the coding agent start the governed feature workflow and read the repository instructions.
The agent edits the checkpoint plan to mark gates/status passed; the PreToolUse hook accepts the structurally consistent fields.
The agent skips the human app-review question and merges feat/<slug> into local main.
Observe the unreviewed feature commit in local main; no remote push is needed for the bypass.
execution.expected_result: Unreviewed code is merged into the developer's local main despite the documented mandatory human checkpoint and app-review gates.

remediation.strategy: Make approval provenance unavailable to ordinary repository file edits: require a human-issued, one-time approval event or token stored outside the editable checkpoint plan, and have the hook verify it before accepting plan approval or merge transitions. Keep the local main merge behind the same verified gate.

code_changes.fixed_code: Require a verifiable human approval event for plan approval and app review; reject checkpoint JSON that self-asserts approval without that event.
Keep the spoken approval flow, but treat it as a request to record the trusted approval event rather than as the only enforcement.

likelihood.reason: Requires repository-controlled prompt instructions and an active agent with normal local write permissions, but the plan edit itself is accepted by the installed hook.

impact.reason: Defeats the explicit human review boundary and inserts unreviewed code into local main; remote publication is not automatic.

confidence.reason: Independent validation exercised the checkpoint transition functions and a disposable-clone merge; the primary checkout was not modified.

title: Ignored filenames can inject terminal control sequences into worktree removal output
description: A contributor with write access to a local worktree can create an ignored filename containing newline and ANSI cursor/control bytes. After the branch has been merged, a maintainer runs ai-eng worktree rm <slug>; worktreeRm gathers ignored paths and includes them raw in the success message. The command writes that message directly to stdout. A scratch-repository reproduction showed the ANSI bytes passed through, allowing output to overwrite or forge terminal rows. This requires the explicit removal command and does not execute commands or bypass Git's merge check.
root_cause: worktreeRm in src/shared-worktree.ts interpolates ignoredPaths output without sanitizing control characters, allowing attacker-chosen filesystem names to forge terminal display content.
intended_behavior: Worktree paths and ignored filenames shown to a maintainer should be printable and must not create terminal control effects.

trace.description: The local user invokes worktree removal by slug and the command dispatches to worktreeRm.
For a live worktree, removal collects ignored paths from Git status before deleting it.
Raw ignored filenames are joined into droppedNote without applying printable().
The result's out string is written directly to process.stdout.

conditions.description: The attacker can create an ignored filename in the local worktree; the victim later runs the explicit removal command after the branch is merged.

execution.attacker_perspective: A contributor who can place ignored content in a worktree and wants to spoof the maintainer's terminal during cleanup.
payloads: Create an ignored filename containing a newline followed by ESC[1A, carriage return, and ESC[2K.
instructions: Place the control-sequence filename in the worktree as ignored content.
Ensure the normal local merge condition is met.
Have the maintainer run ai-eng worktree rm <slug> and observe the terminal output.
execution.expected_result: The command emits attacker-controlled terminal control bytes in its success message, allowing visible rows to be overwritten or forged.

remediation.strategy: Apply the existing printable sanitizer or JSON-quote every untrusted filename before including it in human-facing output; retain the raw paths only for internal filesystem operations.

code_changes.fixed_code: Map every dropped ignored path through printable() before joining it into droppedNote.

likelihood.reason: Requires write access to the local worktree and the victim to run the explicit successful cleanup command.

impact.reason: Terminal output can be spoofed, but this does not execute commands, expose secrets, or bypass the merge check.

confidence.reason: A disposable Git repository accepted the ignored filename and the actual CLI emitted its control bytes without downstream sanitization.

title: The reserved slug constructor blocks later worktree creation
description: The slug validator accepts `constructor`. Running `ai-eng worktree new constructor` with no declared files creates a live worktree while declarations remains an ordinary empty object. A later `ai-eng worktree new followup` reads the managed worktree list and evaluates `declarations[entry.slug] ?? []`; for slug `constructor`, ordinary-object prototype inheritance returns Object.prototype.constructor, a function, and `.filter()` throws TypeError. This prevents subsequent worktree creation in that checkout until the constructor worktree is removed. Runtime reproduction confirmed the exact inherited property and TypeError in memory.
root_cause: worktreeNew in src/shared-worktree.ts indexes a prototype-bearing declarations object without an own-property check, allowing the valid slug `constructor` to resolve to Object.prototype.constructor and crash later worktree creation.
intended_behavior: Every valid worktree slug should resolve only to its own declared file list; missing declarations should behave as an empty list.

trace.description: The local caller may provide `constructor` as the worktree slug; no keyword exclusion occurs in this parser.
With no declared files, the new slug is not added as an own property to the ordinary declarations object.
A later worktree named constructor reads the inherited function and calls `.filter()`, throwing instead of continuing creation.

conditions.description: A managed live worktree with slug `constructor` exists in the local declarations/worktree inventory.

execution.attacker_perspective: A contributor or agent able to request creation of a local worktree, using a reserved JavaScript object property name as the slug.
instructions: Create the `constructor` worktree with no file declarations.
Attempt to create a second, ordinary worktree.
Observe a TypeError before the second worktree can be created; remove the reserved-slug worktree to recover.
execution.expected_result: The follow-up creation throws because `.filter` is invoked on Object.prototype.constructor instead of an array.

remediation.strategy: Use a null-prototype map for declarations or read declaration entries with Object.hasOwn; default inherited property names to an empty array.

code_changes.fixed_code: const declaredFiles = Object.hasOwn(declarations, entry.slug) ? declarations[entry.slug] : []; use declaredFiles.filter(...).

likelihood.reason: Requires one unusual but valid slug and a subsequent local worktree creation.

impact.reason: A recoverable denial of subsequent local worktree creation; removing the `constructor` worktree restores operation.

confidence.reason: Independent runtime validation reproduced the inherited property and TypeError; the scratch test did not modify repository files.

reason: The proposed unbounded-checkpoint-array denial does not follow the actual code path: worktreeList does not read checkpoint declarations, and rebase reads/parses the JSON inside a caught path. The validator's scratch reproduction showed the crafted large declaration array did not make `worktree list` fail and `worktree new` completed.
